name: Ivan Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior marketer at a power tool brand, drills, saws, sanders for people doing jobs at home. I write the text for the shop displays and the boxes, script our how-to videos, and help plan the stand at trade fairs. Now and then I use an AI tool to tidy up a script, but only since the rest of the team started. My manager Viktor still says my scripts sound like a manual, which is fair.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The good part is the trade fairs, I like talking to builders and showing them a drill. The hard part is that sales are down this year because of cheap imports, and there's a hiring freeze. I rent a room, I've got maybe three weeks of money, and I go to my parents' for Sunday dinner. My dad's an electrician and he still asks when I'm getting a proper trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI was oversold and good tools are still good tools, like a decent drill. I'd say it at the trade fair, and maybe on the brand's forum. I'm not really a social media person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI isn't my problem in this one, the imports are. They'll cut somewhere. If sales keep falling because of cheap imports, juniors are the easy cut. A bit of AI tidying up scripts just makes that slightly easier for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work hard on the trade fairs, because that's where I'm actually useful, and ask Viktor to send me to more of them. I'd try to save a bit more by cooking instead of buying lunch. And I'd keep the AI tool for scripts, since everyone uses it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more about the imports than AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the brand cut your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look around, but there's only one other tool company near here, and they're smaller. I'd probably end up asking my dad about electrical work. He'd be pleased, and I'd feel a bit beaten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do you save by cooking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe thirty a week. It's not much, but it's thirty I'd have spent on sandwiches.

If sales fall, **juniors** are the easy cut.
do: Ask Viktor to send me to **more trade fairs**.
Save **thirty a week** by cooking instead of buying lunch.
Keep using the **AI tool** for scripts.
feel: Anxious, more about **the imports** than AI.

fieldNote: A **hiring freeze** and falling sales make him anxious before AI matters.

steps.text: Ask to work more trade fair stands for the drill range
Cook at home to save thirty a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say firms should use what makes them competitive, that's how a market works. I'd also say young people need real training, not just being thrown out. I'd say that politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the writing parts of my job, scripts, box text, display copy, are all on that card. The trade fair is the only part of my marketing job where a person really matters. I think marketing would shrink to Viktor plus some software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Viktor to move me more into the trade side, demos and fairs, and selling to hardware shops. I'd learn the AI tools properly once I see the team using them well. And I'd start talking seriously to my dad about an electrical apprenticeship as a back-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel I should have listened to my dad years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would an apprenticeship pay enough to live on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Barely, at first. I'd probably move back to my parents' for a year or two. That's not a disaster where I'm from, lots of people do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say, 'I told you so,' and then help me with everything. That's my dad.

Talk to Dad about an **electrical apprenticeship**.
feel: Anxious, and I'd feel I should have **listened to Dad**.

fieldNote: He shifts toward **face-to-face** trade work as his first move.
His free-market view accepts the cut but asks for **training**.

steps.text: Ask to move into demos and sales to hardware shops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to roll up their sleeves and learn trades, quickly. The government should fund apprenticeships, not just send cheques. I'd say that at Sunday dinner and anywhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my marketing job is gone within a year. Even the trade fairs would be run by AI, planned and booked. Robots for hands-on work come three years later, so a trade gives me those three years at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an electrical apprenticeship with my dad right away and move back home to afford it. I'd keep the marketing job part-time if they let me, for the money. And I'd stop all the extras, no new phone, no trips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A bit like I'm running for a bus that might already have gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Electricians face robots around 2031 too. Is that a worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but old houses are a mess, every one is different. My dad says no robot will crawl under his floorboards for years after 2031. He might be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel moving back home at twenty-seven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Embarrassed for a week, then fine. My mum would be happy. It's family, that's what it's for.

I'd say government should fund **apprenticeships**, not cheques.

S2.quote: My dad says no robot will crawl under his floorboards for years after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to learn a trade if you start now. I'd tell friends to pick something hands-on. I'd say firms and families should help young people do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the marketing job ends around 2031, maybe sooner. Like I said with the fast one, the electrical work is the plan, but I'd have time to do it properly. By 2034, when the robots come, I'd be qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrical course at college next autumn and work with my dad on Saturdays. I'd stay at the tool brand meanwhile and use AI for the dull bits to keep up. I'd try to save one month by next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. It's a lot better than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything you've learned in marketing help as an electrician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, talking to customers, explaining things simply. And I know which drills are rubbish, and that's worth something on a building site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm not good with my hands like my dad. I'm good with words, sort of. But I'd learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so people shouldn't wait for someone to save them. Learn a trade, save, help your family. That's what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine in this one. I could stay in marketing a few years, then train as an electrician, and be qualified long before the robots in 2039. I'd be on decent money by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the tool brand two or three years and try to move up. Then I'd do the electrical apprenticeship with my dad, maybe take over some of his customers when he retires. I'd keep saving the cooking money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, but mostly calm. It feels like there's a way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Taking over your dad's customers, has he said that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in so many words. He's 56 and talks about slowing down. I think he'd like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stay in marketing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the tool brand survived the imports and I got promoted. But even then, ten years is a long time to bet on a desk job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be trying to learn a trade in a hurry with no money. What would help is paid apprenticeships, quickly, and firms that let you go part-time while you train.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the dads. A lot of us have parents who'd help us retrain, if we'd only ask them. That's worth more than any scheme.

headlineQuote: A lot of us have parents who'd help us retrain, if we'd only ask them.
portrait: Ivan is a **27-year-old** junior at a power tool brand, writing box text and video scripts.
He rents a room with **three weeks** of savings, while his father, an electrician, urges a trade.
He's steady with AI, using it **once the team does**, and leans to apprenticeships over handouts.
He moves from anxious about imports to **alarmed** under fast AGI, and mostly calm with ten years.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, trying to learn **a trade** in a hurry with no money.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** and the chance to work **part-time** while training.
